questions.stem_md: Which title did the Kushana kings adopt to claim a high, god-like status?

options.text_md: Devaputra
Piyadassi
Mahamatta
Gahapati

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Devaputra. Devaputra means son of god. Piyadassi is the epithet found in Ashokan inscriptions, a mahamatta was an officer, and a gahapati was a household head.

questions.stem_md: Which group of powerful local lords was important to the working of Gupta rule?

options.text_md: Vellalar
Samantas
Satthavahas
Dhamma mahamattas

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Samantas. The Guptas depended on samantas. Vellalar were large landowners of the Tamil country, satthavahas were traders, and the mahamattas served Ashoka.

questions.stem_md: For which question would a land-grant inscription be more useful to a historian than a Jataka story?

options.text_md: How villagers felt about a king's heavy taxes
What peasants said to one another at harvest time
The exact pay of Mauryan soldiers
Who received rights over a village's produce after a royal gift

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Who received rights over a village's produce after a royal gift. A grant records who was given what, so it can show who held rights over the produce of the village after the gift. Stories hint at feelings and tensions; neither source gives the exact pay of soldiers.

questions.stem_md: The iron-tipped ploughshare spread in the Ganga and Kaveri valleys, but in drier regions the hoe stayed in use. What does this best suggest?

options.text_md: New techniques spread unevenly, depending on soil and conditions, so production did not rise in the same way everywhere
The hoe was a more advanced tool than the iron ploughshare
Farmers in drier regions did not grow any crops
Iron ploughshares came into use in every region at the same time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** New techniques spread unevenly, depending on soil and conditions, so production did not rise in the same way everywhere. Different tools suited different land, so gains in production varied from place to place. The other options contradict the evidence or claim far more than it shows.

questions.stem_md: A prashasti says a king defeated every ruler of a region, yet coins of one of those rulers go on being issued for many years afterwards. What is the best interpretation?

options.text_md: The coins must be later forgeries
The poem proves that the ruler was never defeated
The claim may be exaggerated, or that ruler may have continued under the king as a subordinate, so the poem cannot be taken at face value
Coins and poems can never be compared with each other

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The claim may be exaggerated, or that ruler may have continued under the king as a subordinate, so the poem cannot be taken at face value. Two kinds of evidence disagree, so a historian looks for an explanation that fits both: praise that overstates, or a defeated ruler who stayed in place as a subordinate. Neither forgery nor a refusal to compare is justified.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student argues that in early India women never controlled land or made grants. Which evidence from this period best challenges that claim?

options.text_md: The Prayaga prashasti composed by Harishena for Samudragupta
A hoard of punch-marked silver coins
An inscription recording a land grant made by Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, who married into the Vakataka family
A fragment of Northern Black Polished Ware

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** An inscription recording a land grant made by Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, who married into the Vakataka family. A single grant made by a woman is enough to challenge the word never. The prashasti, the coins and the pottery do not concern a woman's control of land.

questions.stem_md: Which of these statements about land grants is an interpretation by historians, and not a detail normally recorded in the grants themselves?

options.text_md: Kings made grants to win allies and extend their influence where their control was weak
The grant was made to a Brahmana or a religious institution
The grant was engraved on copper plates
The grant names the ruler who made the gift

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Kings made grants to win allies and extend their influence where their control was weak. The plates record who gave what to whom. Why a king gave land is inferred, and is debated; the three other statements describe contents or form of the record.

questions.stem_md: In the Tamil Sangam texts, large landowners were called ___ and ploughmen were called ___.
questions.solution_md: The Sangam texts call large landowners vellalar and ploughmen uzhavar; slaves were called adimai.

questions.stem_md: Match each term from the study of early rural society and towns with its meaning.

options.text_md: Gahapati
Vellalar
Agrahara
Shreni

match_right.text_md: A guild of craftspeople or merchants
Large landowners in the Tamil country
A Pali term for a household head who controlled its land and workers

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each term is paired with its usual meaning in the chapter.

questions.stem_md: Why do historians disagree about the reasons for land grants? Give two explanations they offer.
questions.solution_md: The cause of the disagreement, then two views.

answer.model_answer_md: Grants are recorded, but their reasons are often not stated, so historians infer them. Some think grants helped extend agriculture to new areas; others think kings made them to win allies and to show their power over a region.

questions.stem_md: Describe two ways in which the Kushana kings tried to claim a high status.
questions.solution_md: The title, and the statues.

answer.model_answer_md: Kushana rulers adopted the title devaputra, or son of god, to suggest a link with the divine. They also had colossal statues of themselves installed at a shrine at Mat near Mathura and in Afghanistan.

questions.stem_md: Why did the iron ploughshare and the transplanting of paddy not benefit all groups in rural society equally? Explain with reference to three groups.
questions.solution_md: Three groups, each linked to how far it gained from better production.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Large landholders, such as the vellalar or the gahapati, gained most, since higher yields from their land and workers raised their wealth.
2. Small peasants gained only if they had land, ploughs and water to use the new methods.
3. Landless labourers and slaves such as the adimai worked harder for the gain of others, so differences in the countryside grew.

questions.stem_md: Examine the evidence for land grants in early India. To what extent do they show that kings were extending agriculture?
questions.solution_md: Evidence, example, two views, and a judgement on how far the evidence allows a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Evidence:** from about the beginning of the Common Era, inscriptions, often on copper plates, record grants to Brahmanas and religious institutions; land given to Brahmanas was called agrahara.
2. **Example:** Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II and married into the Vakataka family, granted land.
3. **First view:** grants brought new land under the plough.
4. **Second view:** kings made grants to win allies and display power, perhaps where their control was weak.
5. **Judgement:** the plates record the gift but rarely the motive, so neither view is certain, and both purposes may have worked together.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined museum guide's notes on an exhibit, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The recipients named in the notes.

**(b)** Evidence of land use before and after.

**(c) (i)** A view chosen, with the limit of the evidence.

**OR (c) (ii)** A view chosen and reasoned from the situation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A group of Brahmanas.

**(b)** Archaeological or other written evidence showing whether the land was waste or forest before the grant and farmed afterwards.

**(c) (i)** (1) It would support the first view, that grants helped bring new land under cultivation, because forested land was not yet farmed. (2) It would not prove it, as the plate does not say that farming followed or what the king intended.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) The second view, because giving land to influential groups could win allies where control was weak. (2) The recipients would then have a stake in the king's success and could support his power locally.

questions.passage_md:
**Notes of a museum guide (imagined), describing an exhibit: a set of copper plates**

The plates are tied together with a ring. They record that a ruler gave a village, with its fields, wells and tanks, to a group of Brahmanas. The text names the ruler, lists the boundaries of the village and says the recipients may enjoy its produce. Visitors often ask why a king would give away a village. I tell them that historians disagree: some think such gifts helped bring new land under cultivation, others think kings used gifts to win the support of influential groups. The plates themselves say what was given, but not why.

children.stem_md: Who received the village according to the guide's notes?
children.solution_md: The recipients named in the notes.

answer.model_answer_md: A group of Brahmanas.

children.stem_md: Name one kind of evidence, other than the plates, that could help a historian test whether grants really brought new land under cultivation.
children.solution_md: Evidence of land use before and after.

answer.model_answer_md: Archaeological or other written evidence showing whether the land was waste or forest before the grant and farmed afterwards.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): A second plate records a grant of forested land to a temple. Which of the two views would this support more, and why? Give two points.
children.solution_md: A view chosen, with the limit of the evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) It would support the first view, that grants helped bring new land under cultivation, because forested land was not yet farmed. (2) It would not prove it, as the plate does not say that farming followed or what the king intended.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which of the two views would a king with weak control over a distant area be more likely to act on, and why? Give two points.
alternatives.solution_md: A view chosen and reasoned from the situation.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The second view, because giving land to influential groups could win allies where control was weak. (2) The recipients would then have a stake in the king's success and could support his power locally.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, a SOYL summary of a kind of royal praise-poem, and answer the questions that follow. *(Summary written by SOYL in its own words for practice; it is not a quotation or translation of any source.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Poet and king as named.

**(b)** The question of authorship applied to what is left out.

**(c) (i)** Two sources for cross-checking.

**OR (c) (ii)** Survival is not reliability.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The poet was Harishena and the king was Samudragupta.

**(b)** Defeats, setbacks or the point of view of the rulers who were overcome, since a poet writing to praise the king would not stress them.

**(c) (i)** (1) Coins of the king and of neighbouring rulers, which may show where each was active. (2) Inscriptions or texts from other regions that mention the same events or rulers.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) Survival shows only that the text lasted, not that its claims are true. (2) The poem still reflects the poet's aim of praising the king, so it needs checking against other evidence.

questions.passage_md:
**SOYL summary of a kind of royal praise-poem**

In the Gupta age, kings had poems of praise cut into stone. One famous example was composed by the court poet Harishena for Samudragupta and is cut on a pillar at Prayaga. Poems of this kind describe the king's qualities and the rulers and peoples he is said to have overcome. The poet belonged to the court and wrote with the king's approval in mind. Historians read such poems for what they say, but they also ask who wrote them and why.

children.stem_md: Name the poet and the king mentioned in the summary.

answer.model_answer_md: The poet was Harishena and the king was Samudragupta.

children.stem_md: Historians ask who wrote such poems and why. Applying that question, what kind of event would such a poem be likely to leave out?
children.solution_md: The question of authorship applied to what is left out.

answer.model_answer_md: Defeats, setbacks or the point of view of the rulers who were overcome, since a poet writing to praise the king would not stress them.

marking_scheme.step: A suitable omission with the reason

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Suggest two other kinds of evidence a historian could use to check the claims of such a poem.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Coins of the king and of neighbouring rulers, which may show where each was active. (2) Inscriptions or texts from other regions that mention the same events or rulers.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The poem has survived on stone for many centuries. Does that make it a reliable record? Give two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Survival shows only that the text lasted, not that its claims are true. (2) The poem still reflects the poet's aim of praising the king, so it needs checking against other evidence.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following was a coastal trading town of the Tamil country, also called Kaveripattinam?

options.text_md: Pataliputra
Ujjayini
Mathura
Puhar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Puhar. Puhar was a port town. Pataliputra, Ujjayini and Mathura were important cities, but they were not on the Tamil coast.

questions.stem_md: Northern Black Polished Ware, found at many urban sites, is

options.text_md: A kind of iron tool
A fine, glossy pottery
A type of coin
A script used on rock edicts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A fine, glossy pottery. Northern Black Polished Ware is a fine, glossy pottery. It is an archaeological find, not a tool, coin or script.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum label describes a copper coin stamped with small symbols but bearing no ruler's name and no portrait. Which judgement is best supported?

options.text_md: It is probably a punch-marked coin, of a type used from about the sixth century BCE, and not an Indo-Greek or Kushana issue
It is probably an Indo-Greek coin, because those carry symbols but no names
It is probably a Kushana gold coin of the first century CE
It must be a Gupta coin, since the Guptas never named themselves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is probably a punch-marked coin, of a type used from about the sixth century BCE, and not an Indo-Greek or Kushana issue. Indo-Greek coins were the first to carry rulers' names and images, and the Kushanas issued gold coins on a large scale. A copper coin with only symbols matches the punch-marked type.

questions.stem_md: A hoard of Roman gold coins is found at a river-mouth town in south India. Which conclusion is best supported by this evidence?

options.text_md: The Roman Empire governed the southern coast
Goods from the region reached Roman markets and were paid for, at least in part, with coins, but the find does not show that Romans ruled the area
Roman traders were the only merchants in the town
The town had no trade with any other region

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Goods from the region reached Roman markets and were paid for, at least in part, with coins, but the find does not show that Romans ruled the area. Coins found in a hoard show that such coins reached the place, which fits trade in valued goods such as pepper. Rule, exclusive trade and the absence of other trade are all claims beyond the find.

questions.stem_md: Coins of one king are found in large numbers at a market town far from his capital. Which inference is the most careful?

options.text_md: He certainly ruled the town directly
The town had no trade with other places
The coins circulated there, probably through trade or payments, but his control over the town needs other evidence
The coins must have been made at that town

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The coins circulated there, probably through trade or payments, but his control over the town needs other evidence. The place where coins are found shows where they travelled, which can happen without political control. A claim of rule needs support from inscriptions or texts.

questions.stem_md: Which further evidence would best help historians decide whether fewer gold coins after about 600 CE reflect a decline in trade?

options.text_md: The purity of Gupta gold coins
The number of mahajanapadas named in Buddhist texts
The date on which Prinsep deciphered Brahmi
Evidence from ports and towns of the same period, such as fewer imported goods or shrinking urban sites

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Evidence from ports and towns of the same period, such as fewer imported goods or shrinking urban sites. Trade can be tested against other traces of exchange and town life from the same period. The other options do not bear on trade after 600 CE.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Finding many coins of a king at a distant town does not prove that he ruled the town.

**Reason (R):** Coins could move from place to place through trade and payments.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since coins travel, where they turn up shows where they went and not necessarily where their issuer ruled.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Not all historians accept the fall in gold coin finds from about 600 CE as proof of declining trade.

**Reason (R):** Gupta gold coins are remarkable for their purity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. The purity of Gupta gold coins is a fact about their quality, whereas the doubt arises because a smaller number of finds can be explained in more than one way.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hoards of Roman coins found in south India prove that the Roman Empire governed the region.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The coins point to trade contacts, not to political rule.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these stages in the history of early Indian coins in the order in which they appear.

options.text_md: Fewer gold coins are found
Gold coins issued on a large scale by the Kushanas
Indo-Greek coins with the names and images of rulers
Punch-marked silver and copper coins

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Punch-marked coins from c. 6th century BCE, Indo-Greek coins next, Kushana gold in the first century CE, and fewer gold coins from about the sixth century CE.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: A coin carries a ruler's portrait and name on one side and a deity on the other. State two things a historian can infer from it and one thing it cannot show.
questions.solution_md: Two inferences and one limit.

answer.model_answer_md: The coin suggests that the ruler issued coins in his own name and image, so he had authority to mint, and that religious symbols mattered in how rulers presented themselves. It cannot show how far his rule extended, since coins travel through trade.

questions.stem_md: What can short donor inscriptions at urban sites tell us about a town, and what can they not tell us?
questions.solution_md: What the donors reveal, and the limit.

answer.model_answer_md: They name donors such as weavers, scribes, carpenters, potters, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, officials and merchants, so they show the range of occupations in a town. They cannot tell us how many people followed each trade or how most townspeople lived.

questions.stem_md: Fewer gold coins are found from about the sixth century CE. Give two reasons why historians hesitate to treat this as proof that trade declined.
questions.solution_md: Two cautions about the evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: Historians disagree about what the fall means. Coins that survive and are found are only a sample, so fewer finds need not mean less trade. Other forms of exchange may also have been used, so coins alone cannot settle the question.

questions.stem_md: An imagined hoard holds punch-marked silver coins and two Indo-Greek coins bearing rulers' portraits and names, but no gold coins. What is the earliest period in which it could have been buried? Give two reasons and one limit of this dating.
questions.solution_md: The latest coin gives the earliest date; older coins can stay in circulation; absence is weak evidence.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. No earlier than the time of the Indo-Greek issues, around the second century BCE, since a hoard cannot be buried before its latest coin was made.
2. The punch-marked silver coins are older, so they were still in use alongside the later ones.
3. Limit: the absence of Kushana gold does not prove burial before the first century CE, because the owner may simply not have held any gold.

marking_scheme.step: Earliest date from the latest coin

questions.stem_md: How far do coins help historians to reconstruct the economy and politics of early India? Support your answer with examples.
questions.solution_md: Examples from different periods, then limits that qualify the answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Early coins:** punch-marked silver and copper coins, from about the sixth century BCE, bear symbols but not rulers' names.
2. **Rulers shown:** Indo-Greek coins first bore rulers' names and images; the Kushanas issued gold coins on a large scale; Gupta gold coins were remarkably pure.
3. **Trade:** hoards of Roman coins in south India point to trade, including in pepper.
4. **Politics:** tribal republics such as the Yaudheyas of Punjab and Haryana issued copper coins.
5. **Limits:** finds are only a sample, and fewer gold coins after about 600 CE may or may not mean less trade, so coins need other evidence.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined diary of an excavation assistant, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The early coin type.

**(b)** Layers and coin types both give relative dates.

**(c) (i)** Two finds, each linked to trade.

**OR (c) (ii)** What it shows and what it cannot.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Punch-marked coins.

**(b)** It lay in the top, later layer, and coins with rulers' heads and names came after punch-marked types, so it is younger than the pottery.

**(c) (i)** (1) Beads of a stone that does not occur near the mound must have been brought from elsewhere. (2) Silver coins in the same layer suggest that coined money was used in exchange, and coins travel between places.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) It tells us that weavers lived in the town and had enough resources to make a donation. (2) It cannot tell us how many weavers there were or how most townspeople lived, since it records only one gift.

questions.passage_md:
**Field diary of an excavation assistant (imagined), a mound beside a river**

The lower layer of today's trench gave fine, glossy black pottery and a handful of silver coins stamped with small symbols but no names. In the same layer we found beads of a stone that does not occur anywhere near the mound. A small stone slab with a few lines of writing was lifted from the middle layer; the supervisor says it records a gift made by a family of weavers. Near the top, a coin bearing a king's head and a name turned up and was bagged separately.

answer.model_answer_md: Punch-marked coins.

children.stem_md: Why should the coin with a king's head and name not be used to date the glossy pottery in the lower layer?
children.solution_md: Layers and coin types both give relative dates.

answer.model_answer_md: It lay in the top, later layer, and coins with rulers' heads and names came after punch-marked types, so it is younger than the pottery.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Using two finds from the diary, explain how historians might infer that the town had trade links.
children.solution_md: Two finds, each linked to trade.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Beads of a stone that does not occur near the mound must have been brought from elsewhere. (2) Silver coins in the same layer suggest that coined money was used in exchange, and coins travel between places.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): What can the slab recording a gift by weavers tell us about the town, and what can it not tell us?
alternatives.solution_md: What it shows and what it cannot.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) It tells us that weavers lived in the town and had enough resources to make a donation. (2) It cannot tell us how many weavers there were or how most townspeople lived, since it records only one gift.

questions.stem_md: For which of these questions would Ashoka's inscriptions be the most useful source?

options.text_md: How much a potter earned in Pataliputra
What villagers thought of Mauryan officials
How many soldiers served in the army
What moral ideas the king wanted his subjects to follow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** What moral ideas the king wanted his subjects to follow. The edicts announce the king's own message. They are poorly placed to answer questions about earnings, popular feeling or army size.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined urban site, short inscriptions record gifts from a washerman's family, a scribe, a potter, a goldsmith and a merchant. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: All the donors belonged to one rich family
The town had no merchants
The town had people in many crafts and occupations, though the inscriptions alone cannot say how large each group was
The town was ruled by a gana

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The town had people in many crafts and occupations, though the inscriptions alone cannot say how large each group was. Different donors point to different occupations. The inscriptions record gifts, not the size of each group, and they say nothing about the form of government.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Inscriptions give a complete and neutral record of life in the past.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Many have been lost or damaged, and they record what their makers wished to say.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three difficulties that historians face in using inscriptions as evidence.
questions.solution_md: Any three difficulties, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Letters may be faintly engraved, damaged or missing, so a reading can be uncertain.
2. Some words have uncertain meanings, and a number of inscriptions have not yet been deciphered or translated.
3. Many more inscriptions existed than survive, and they record what their makers wished to say, so everyday life is often left out.
